text: All right. Good afternoon, everyone. I call this October 7th meeting of the Curriculum and Instruction Committee to order. I'm Dr. Rasheed. I'm the chair. I appreciate everyone's presence here today, and what a beautiful day it is. The purpose of the meeting is to discuss a couple of things. First, we have to approve our previous meeting's minutes. And then we have some information items, which is updating the Policy 5430, use of

generative AI, and Regulation 5430.2, privacy and data protection when using AI. The other one is middle school schedule proposals and feedback, and program of studies changes for 2027, 2028. I understand we do not have public comment, so I will move on. All right. We need to approve the minutes from September 2nd. I can't believe we are almost halfway through October.

Has everyone had a chance to review the minutes? And if so, are there any changes? All right. I entertain a motion to approve the minutes from September 2nd. So moved. Second. Awesome. Thank you. That was moved by Mr. Svensen and seconded by Ms. Chernov. All those in favor say aye. Aye. Aye. All those then say nay, whoever is opposed, which is none. All right. Let's go ahead and move on to

information item 4.01. I will turn it over to Mr. Slevin to present, who is Assistant Superintendent of Teaching and Learning. Thanks. Thank you, Dr. Rasheed and committee members. I'm here tonight on behalf of Mr. Aaron Smith, our Chief Information Officer, in partnership with proposed updates to LCPS Policy 5430, use of generative artificial intelligence. As you all know, LCPS has an existing policy on the use of

generative artificial intelligence, and as our system has matured and learned over the past couple of years, we're coming to the committee and then eventually the full board with a proposed update related to this tool. So this update modernizes and updates our guidance regarding the use of personally identifiable information with generative AI tools by recognizing the safeguards that now are available on LCPS-approved enterprise-managed AI platforms.

Since the original policy language was drafted, LCPS has expanded its use of enterprise AI solutions that include contractual, technical, and privacy protections designed specifically for educational and business environments. So speaking specifically about tools such as Gemini and Copilot. The previous approach emphasized avoiding the use of PII with AI tools because many of our consumer AI applications use submitted data to train public models and may

not adequately protect students' or staff information. Today, LCPS-approved enterprise AI applications operate under strict contractual agreements that restrict how data is used, prohibit the use of customer data for model training, and provide privacy and security controls consistent with LCPS requirements. As a result, there's now a significant distinction between approved enterprise platforms and consumer AI applications, and the policy that we have

should clearly reflect that difference, as well as the accompanying regulation. What is changing? PII may be used within LCPS enterprise-managed and approved generative AI applications when there is legitimate educational or business purposes and when employees follow applicable privacy and security requirements. The prohibition remains in place for non-LCPS managed consumer or unauthorized AI applications for which data protections cannot be verified or enforced by LCPS.

So why, do we want to do this? How do we think this is going to benefit staff and students? This will enable staff to use AI-approved tools more effectively for instructional planning, administrative tasks, data analysis, communication support, and operational efficiency. It'll reduce confusion by providing clear guidance on when this information may be used and when it may not be used. It aligns policy with the current practices for all our enterprise technology environments. As you are aware, for example, Google Drive and Google Apps for

Education are widely used within LCPS. It aligns policy with the current practices for our enterprise technology environment, encourages responsible innovation while maintaining strong protections for students, staff, and family information. We do want to note that privacy and security protections remain in place. Approved LCPS AI applications undergo review to ensure compliance with federal and state student privacy requirements and division policies.

And our enterprise-managed tools include protections intended to prevent customer data from being used to train public AI models and to limit data sharing with third parties. DDI and Teaching and Learning maintain oversight of approved AI tools and conduct ongoing review of these technologies together. So in terms of FERPA and compliance considerations, this update does not relax student privacy obligations. Sharing information in unauthorized or non-LCPS managed AI applications remains prohibited.

Unauthorized disclosure of student information through non-approved AI tools may constitute a FERPA-related incident and could require notification to affected students and families. This change establishes a clear approved versus unapproved framework rather than a blanket restriction of use of AI when it comes to PII. So today, I'm happy to answer any specific questions or feedback or between now and the next time we bring this back. But we would like to send this out to the public

for feedback and be able to address any issues that may be raised when we do that. Thank you, Mr. Slevin. I have no questions or comments, but I'll turn it over to my colleagues. Any questions or comments? Yes, Ms. Chernov. Thank you, Chair Rasheed. I'm on board with all of these changes. I think we had a really nice, fulsome conversation at the full board level to queue this up. So I'm grateful that we had that context and background knowledge.

I do think we are wading in murkier waters as it applies to AI with PII. So I'm comfortable with it personally, but I know we are hearing from families that have reservations about it. So I'm wondering if now that we are switching from approved, if there is an opportunity for adding to the regulation a section on how families will be notified and if there's any opt-out availability.

The people that seem against it seem really fearful and against it, so just something for the committee to think about in terms of how we're going to notify families. are we doing this for all students, or would this really just apply at first to the pilot, correct? So we're not talking about student use of generative AI tools. Okay. access and intervention structures, principal perceptions of schedule flexibility and alignment to school priorities, implementation of dedicated time for advisory, intervention, and enrichment, student access to a broader range of elective opportunities, and indicators related to student experience, such as a sense of belonging. as workable but in need of refinement. Additionally, there was no single preferred schedule or model. of the drivers of why we did this work in this important context to understand the discussions that were held. Next slide, please. So first up, and Dr. Grubbs is going to be going further in depth about this topic. Our principals really have asked for an increase in creative elective offerings

for their students. And the current offerings they feel are more rigid in the instructional schedule. So he will be talking about that. schedule, the traditional middle school instructional schedule, does not have the time, where they could be creative with their own buildings, to have intervention time for their students. So this slide might be confusing, and the left side shows parameters that our middle school leaders have that can be loose or flexible.

And then the right side shows what has to be tight or absolutely fixed within division expectations. So if you ever hear us say what's loose, tight, or what's flexible or adaptive versus something that's fixed, that's what we refer to. So I'd like to first touch upon advisory. We have shared with our leaders and given the direction that advisory, if you look

on the right-hand side, absolutely is a middle school structure that is in place across all 18 middle schools, and at a minimum, two times a week, all students have advisory. But then if you look on the left side, what would the flexibility be? Because each school is very diverse and very different. Schools can determine the duration that they may need for that advisory lesson. They can also assign the advisory lessons.

They use the curriculum that is provided by LCPS But also have advisory committees that help them come up with lessons. And then the next bullet down on the left side, interdisciplinary teams, if you ever hear us say IT teams, those are teams of teachers that meet to talk about students and do a lot of the MTSS work. So those have to be flexible, because not all of those teachers are off teaching at the same time.

So schools can schedule those team meetings before school, after school, or during school, but they're flexible in when they may do that. And then if you look three bullets down on the right, something that is absolutely a middle school staple are CLTs, and they meet weekly. So a collaborative learning team and the planning time together is something that is a shared division expectation and absolutely tight with all of our schools.

Something that I talked about earlier, the intervention time, on the right-hand side, is we do have division-wide expectations about students getting interventions. But on the left side, you'll see flexible scheduling models and parameters. Schools have flexibility on where and when they may schedule those intervention times. So the support blocks, intervention structures, those are flexible based on the needs of the instructional schedule within the building.

And then something else I really would like to highlight on this, and I know you can all read it, is something that Mildred talked about with schedule alignment. We have encouraged our schools to be flexible where they can be with their schedules without blowing up the entire instructional schedule. But the schedule alignment, they can't impact the staffing needs of another building when schools may share staff.

So we do, in this school division, have a lot of itinerant staff. And what we've learned from schedule models at Trailside and Watson Mountain with their schedule pilots is that when you have a different schedule model, you may impact the instructional schedules of other schools. So that's why schedule alignment is on the tight, the fixed side of

the screen. And then also gifted. We do have gifted services that we absolutely are tight on because they are a division-wide expectation and also have parameters within VDOE. So I hope this is a good graphic to explain what might be loose and flexible for our leaders, but also what is fixed and tight.

So before we get into some of the proposals that we are making, we wanted to address an idea that floated around a lot at the beginning of this process, and that based on feedback we received from principals and others, was one that we ultimately didn't really pursue, which is the idea of an elective wheel or exploratory wheel. That's a great way to meet that need of expanding elective choices. But something that our principals told us a lot was that that really creates just another structure in the schedule.

And when trying to think about how we can have more flexibility, how we can increase more access to interventions, that really creates just another structure for schools to have to navigate to be able to do that. So really where we landed was in a more consistent structure. Currently, let's take sixth grade, for example, a student would have a half block resource and a half block music class. They would also have a semester of art and a semester of introduction to computer

applications as well. And so you have these 45-minute structures, and you have semester structures, and those things can't be mixed and matched. So it really does lock the school into certain ways of doing things. What we are proposing is moving all of those to, say, a 45-minute block. And what that allows the school to do is to maybe pair resource and arts together, or ICA and band, and to use their staffing for interventions more efficiently and

effectively to place those blocks where they need them. And to also make sure that we don't remove a student's access to electives. So that one of those 45-minute blocks might be pulled out to create an intervention block for a student, but that doesn't mean that they lose an entire elective block, that they still would have access to some of those blocks as well. So we really feel that this structure does a lot of the things that we want to do.

It preserves access to electives while also giving schools more flexibility to implement interventions, which are the two big priorities that we saw so far. The next slide shares, as Mr. Slevin said, some considerations we would like to make for how we might address some other needs that schools identified as part of this process. And on the left are some ideas for how we might enhance our elective

offerings. And as Ms. Charlie Green showed in one of our slides, really staffing is one of the key factors that we need to address if we want to expand elective offerings for students. So this proposal would, over a period of years, this shows three years, it could be faster than three years or less than three years, takes the middle school class size from 23.7 down to 23.1. And so a phased approach over the next three years is on the screen

there, that in FY28, the target class size in middle school would be 23.5, in FY29 23.3, and in FY30 23.1. At the conclusion of that, we would generate about 26 new FTEs in our middle schools. It would reduce the average middle school teacher load from 142 students to 138, so a small reduction in that, still a little bit different than high school.

And for a total cost, that would be about $3.4 million, 3.495, $3.5 million at full implementation. Again, that's the full plan over those three years. So it's about $1.165 million per year over three years. On the right-hand side is how we might address intervention.

So, by far the biggest request that we have is for the addition of a math resource teacher at the middle school level. Currently, six of our middle schools have a full-time math resource teacher, and this proposal would add a math resource teacher at all middle schools. So this is 12 new math resource teacher positions to give each school one of these positions. And those positions spend about 50% of their time providing direct

intervention to students and 50% of their time working with CLTs and coaching teachers in effective math instruction. So that would add 12 new FTEs, and that would be about $1.68 million at full implementation. So if we take year one of the staffing of lowering the class size and this proposal, that would be in FY28, $2.845 million to achieve those two goals.

We wanted to, on the next slide, show you what the impact of this would be over time at three of our middle schools. So this is showing the class size reduction. First is a small middle school in LCPS, school two is an average size middle school in LCPS, and school three is a large middle school in LCPS. And so by reducing the class size, we do open up the possibility for schools to add some additional elective opportunities for students.

would see these things increase. But I think schools would be going at different rates and at different speeds, but always with a movement towards offering more courses and more choice and opportunities for students.
